entry.title: The Best Personalized Christmas Gifts
entry.summary: From monogrammed pajamas to bespoke Oreos.
entry.content:
Personalization (whether you’re monogramming a luggage tag with your mom’s initials or building a custom LEGO Minifigure that looks exactly like your cousin Sarah) is the way to make sure a recipient knows you actually thought about your gift and didn’t just run to the mall in a Christmas Eve panic. On that note, I encourage you to make your personalized-gift decisions quickly, as many brands increase shipping times by a number of weeks once customization is involved. Purchasing these gifts in November is definitely the safest bet; as the weeks progress, I’ll update this page with last-minute shipping information.

Below, you’ll find a number of nameplate jewelry options, naturally, as well as a monogrammed tote bag, robe, and cozy blanket. There are also a few curveballs, like a slightly Victorian photo-portrait pendant, a box of bespoke Oreos, and a tomato-scented candle with room on the label for whichever heartfelt message or tongue-in-cheek in-joke you choose. Methods of customization can vary; in most cases you’ll find a button that says “personalize” or something similar when you’ve clicked through to the retailer’s product page. I’ve taken note of any instances where extra work on your part is required.

Yeti’s excellent insulated Rambler mugs can be customized with images and text on the brand’s website and will be the envy of Prospect Park.

A smart-looking miniature flatware set that their parents will also treasure.

We love Casetify’s cases for both their looks and utility. The customization options on this one range from subtle to loud, so you can truly tailor your choices to the recipient’s personality.

Sporty tween boys will appreciate Gatorade’s reusable water bottle that can be personalized with different patterns, accent colors, and text.

The quintessential preppy tote bag, as carried by Carolyn Bessette — but customized with your recipient’s initials or perhaps an in-joke you two share.

Did you know that you can build a bear online? In addition to whatever unique clothing and accessories you choose, each bear ships with a custom birth certificate displaying its new parent’s name.

I particularly like the idea of turning old family photos into puzzles, but recent ones work too.

These little LEGO people are almost as fun to make as they are to receive. We like to give them to our dads.

Now she’ll be sending it with extra pizzazz.

A luxurious (yet not extravagantly priced) blanket that can be monogrammed with up to ten characters.

An opulent lipstick in a metal case that can be engraved for an extra $5.

A box full of Oreos customized with their name and their preferred filling and sprinkles.

A tube full of M&M’s with their initials on them, in a custom color scheme of your choosing.

Everybody’s favorite water bottle can now be customized.

A slightly Victorian way for them to always keep their baby close.

Christen their new digs with a personalized towel.

A warm hat for the cold days to come.

An apology in the form of Emi Jay’s most popular claw clip.

Build him a custom multi-tool in his favorite colors, then engrave it.

A Donatella-approved trinket tray.

Upgrade their setup with a custom controller.

A non-novelty bag charm.

Don’t overcomplicate it. Catbird makes simple and minimal alphabet charms, whereas Susan Alexandra offers a few quirkier designs.

A slightly bonkers but very fun phone case with her name bedazzled in cursive, alongside other accoutrements.

Get him a monogrammed robe in a seasonally appropriate forest-green tartan.

Adorable customized stationery that they likely wouldn’t splurge on themselves.

A classy jewelry case to keep precious pieces safe.

Gohar World’s playful rubber gloves might help stop the plates from piling up and can be personalized with a choice of embroidered motifs and monograms.

The apron worn by our fallen Test Kitchen heroes comes with optional monogramming.

Comfy (and, in some circles at least, trendy) custom slides for his daily beach walk.

Sézane’s crisp button-down (with a small monogram that’s as unfussy as Jane Birkin herself) is a subtle way to signal her good taste.

A new season has begun, and here’s how they can show support for the reigning champs.

Monogrammed pajamas for when they’re working on their projects (or just watching their shows) indoors this winter.

All that chopping will be made easier with this handsome customized teak board.

A professional-looking laptop case that’ll protect that naked Macbook they’ve been stuffing into a tote bag.

The silk pillowcase that our beauty writer Tembe Denton-Hurst has been resting her head on for years.

A monogrammed set of magnetic capsules they can decant all their lotions and potions into.

And if they have a beloved pet, Janie Korn also makes dog and cat portrait candles to match.

Alex Mill’s tote bag is a favorite of ours for work and play, and it holds everything. The custom lettering is hand-painted in Brooklyn.

Email Lindquist after placing your order to add a gold or embossed monogram for an extra $10.

Introduce her to the dolls you played with as a kid by completely customizing one that she’ll love just as much.

If they’re known to bring bottles of Veuve to the gathering, this customized cooler box is designed to keep two of them chilled.

Hades hand-knits these alphabet-letter wool sweaters in Scotland. If they wouldn’t be caught dead in a polyester blend, they’ll appreciate receiving one of these.

A monogrammed leather cuff-link container with room for their two favorite pairs.

entry.title: 60 Superb Christmas Stockings
entry.summary: Bedecked with bows and ruffles, stripes and checks, pom-poms, and even lights.
entry.content:
The Strategist staff has plenty of ideas about how best to stuff a stocking, but let’s not forget about the stocking itself. Just like a tree skirt, Christmas stockings are a fundamental piece of holiday décor — one that confers a sense of festive anticipation all season long before playing a crucial role on Christmas morning, when it’s called upon to contain all sorts of delightful goodies. The vintage stockings of yore have their charm, of course, but if you’re looking to update the ones bequeathed from Grandma, there’s a vast array of stylish options out there, whether they’re hand-knit and hand-embroidered, trimmed with fur, or covered in geometric shapes or colorful stripes. Below, we’ve rounded up a slew of stockings that deserve a spot on your mantelpiece, including ones made from velvet, linen, wool, and tartan and bedecked with bows, ribbons, pom-poms, and lights. (There’s even one shaped like a bone so your dog doesn’t feel left out.)

entry.title: My Hunt for a Smart, Tailored, Working Girl–Fantasy Blazer
entry.summary: It takes a lot of work to look tailored (so I learned).
entry.content:
Since watching Working Girl for the first time around a decade ago, I have wanted a blazer like Melanie Griffith’s or Sigourney Weaver’s. (More than I wanted to tell a stranger who reminded me of Harrison Ford about my “head for business and bod for sin.”) Not necessarily a shoulder-padded blazer exactly as worn by Tess McGill or Katharine Parker, but one that was tailored to perfection. I’d like nothing more than to look as smart and capable as they did.

I came to understand the limitations of something “tailored” off-the-rack during this hunt. I’m curvier and shorter, and anything described as “slim” or “fitted” required me to size up to a 12 or a large (rather than my usual size 10 or medium). I was looking for something with a little bit of a nipped-in waist too. As I learned, the amount of tailoring you’re getting can vary by price — but J.Crew and Buck Mason alike offered flattering darts and back seams. Generally, you’re dealing in more synthetic blends when buying cheaper. There’s a range of blazers from $100 to $575 below — and I considered prices when deciding between favorites. Here’s everything I tried. For reference, I’m about five-two.

I let out a sigh of disappointment the minute I slipped an arm into this. It was so tight in the sleeve that any slight arm movement pinched. For someone who talks with their hands, it was a problem.

The Diish Chiara Black Cinched Blazer is better suited for happy hour at 6 p.m. than meeting with your boss at 10 a.m. I can picture Logan Roy telling me I’m not a Serious Person while wearing it. Especially as the buttons kept coming undone.

We’ve recommended Artizia’s Effortless Pant repeatedly; illustrator Edith Young called it “a work pant for the ages.” Just as promising-sounding was the Standout Blazer — a single-breasted, notch-lapeled wonder. Or so I thought. Aritzia uses its trademarked Eversential, which it describes as a “stretch fabric that holds its form” made with polyester and Lenzing Ecovero viscose sourced from a Portuguese mill. I think I’d prefer the feeling of its Crepette (it’s available in the fabric) — as I found that Eversential wrinkles easily. And I know I don’t have a model’s proportions, but the fit was wildly off. I didn’t even attempt to close it — for fear that a button would pop off.

Aligne topped our senior Lauren Ro’s hunt for an overcoat last November (passerbys gave her approving once-overs when she was in the George Wrap Coat), so I had high expectations for the brand’s Daphne Double Breasted Blazer and Ponte Blazer. Neither fit me as I hoped they would. Trying to figure out the Daphne’s concealed placket was harder than I imagined — even as someone who’s mastered the art of zipping herself up without needing a wire hanger. I couldn’t get any of the buttons buttoned. If I could’ve, I would’ve gotten a U.K. size 16 (equivalent to a U.S. 12) rather than a U.K. size 14 (equivalent to a U.S. 10), but it was sold out over the course of my hunt. And the Ponte (in a U.K. 14/U.S. 10) did me no favors. The seam at the waistline didn’t hit at my natural waist (it was just an inch too high).

Maybe wishful thinking on my part, but I hoped this might be the closest thing to an American Gigolo Armani suit, as it’s inspired by the silhouettes of the ‘70s. Alas, it was not to be. The longer I stared at myself in it, the more questions I had, including Am I really that broad-shouldered? It was just too boxy. If you’re considering, size down (this is the size 10).

All I kept thinking when wearing the Banana Republic Slim Italian Lightweight Wool Blazer was it’s fine. Not bad by any means. Just something nondescript for your first internship. It didn’t help that it was crushed in my full clothing rack. The fabric showed wrinkles more obviously than others I tried.

While more waist-accentuating than the Banana Republic Slim Blazer, the Quince Italian Wool Stand Collar Blazer was just okay. This might be a selling point to you: It’s vaguely Rag & Bone-y. Annoyingly, the collar flopped constantly.

The waist-defining princess seams of Modern Citizen’s Marina Wool-Blend Sculpted Blazer do everything they’re supposed to do. What an hourglass shape they gave me. If only I didn’t feel like an overstuffed grape when fully buttoned up. It would’ve reminded me of Christian Dior’s 1947 Bar Suit otherwise.

I let out a squeal when I opened the package containing Argent’s Collared Blazer. It’s a painfully beautiful garment. To my great disappointment, it was a smidge tight. Even when I sized up to a 12. It took all my willpower to get through the row of buttons. I usually buy blazers with the intention of wearing them open, but for $575, I ought to be able to keep it closed.

I’ve said it once and I’ll say it again: The inner textile nerd in me appreciates the good old-fashioned craftsmanship of Buck Mason. The quality’s there with the Hollywood Blazer. The Shetland wool it’s made of comes from Yorkshire’s Abraham Moon & Sons (established in 1837). You can’t help feeling like you’ve moved up a tax bracket in it. That said, it reminds me of a sport coat a thoughtful boyfriend would put over your shoulders when waiting for a B train after a wedding. You know, too big. Had I known better, I would’ve called in a size eight instead of the ten.

[Editor’s note: Some sizes are sold out right now, but you can sign up to receive an email when your size is back in stock.]

Buck Mason’s Felted Wool Shrunken Graduate Blazer harkens back to the tailoring of the 1940s. I worried that the twice-boiled merino wool would have sweater-blazer connotations. It doesn’t! I’m a retired, distinguished linguistics professor in this. It made me want to talk in a Transatlantic accent.

From the new Uniqlo:C by Clare Waight Keller (Uniqlo’s creative director since 2024; formerly, Pringle of Scotland and Givenchy) comes the Double Face Tailored Jacket. It was delivered at the eleventh hour yesterday. I texted a photo to my mom (who wouldn’t hesitate to tell me if something fits incorrectly) for a second opinion, and she replied with a restrained “looking good.” It’s less relaxed than I imagined in the Medium. It’s officially “unisex,” but available in women’s sizes XXS to XXL. I liked the easily rollable, buttonless sleeves and the functional pockets (only the Buck Mason Felted Wool Shrunken Graduate Blazer has them too).

Oh, how wonderfully Admiral Crepe (blend of a blend of polyester and triacetate) drapes. It did miracles for me. Never did I feel it was too soft. It held the form of the Cutaway Jacket. Impeccable clean lines. But it ain’t cheap at $495.

I can’t remember the last time a mall brand got tailoring this right. J.Crew’s Margeaux Blazer has sharp padding, great nipping at the waist, and it hugged me in all the right places. I felt like I belonged on the cover of a first-edition Dress for Success.

entry.title: Can Red Light Help Me Sleep Better?
entry.summary: There’s a difference between helping and not hurting.
entry.content:
If you’ve opened Instagram, TikTok, or any other social-media platform where wellness types congregate, you know red-light therapy is everywhere. The products range from ubiquitous red-light masks to giant glowing panels of red light. We’ve covered plenty of those products for skin care, hair growth, and pain relief here at the Strategist — and in certain use cases, there is decent evidence that red-light therapy can be effective.

But lately, I’ve seen more and more claims from red-light devices designed to help you sleep better. I’ve been hearing about red light for sleep for a while now. The theory is that because blue light — the type of light the sun emits — signals to our brains that they should be awake and alert, and because some research suggests that too much exposure to blue light at night can disrupt your sleep, red light can help promote sleep because it is furthest from blue on the visible light spectrum. It’s exactly the kind of science-y claim that seems plausible enough to a relative layperson like myself. So I called up an actual expert, S. Justin Thomas, Ph.D., associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral neurobiology and director of the behavioral sleep medicine clinic at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. And for good measure, I tried a couple of red-light lamps myself.

Right now, not much. There haven’t been many clinical trials, Thomas tells me, so there isn’t any strong evidence supporting red-light therapy for sleep. But there is some credibility to the idea that red light’s longer wavelengths may be better for sleep than blue light’s shorter wavelengths. “The way the circadian system operates is that we have specialized cells in our eyes that transmit light information back to a part of our brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus,” Thomas says. “And that in turn sends a signal to produce melatonin or not.” So when our eyes take in blue light — or light that’s close on the visible light spectrum, like green light — melatonin production is suppressed. Darkness in the evening signals to our brains through our retinas that it’s getting close to bedtime, and slowly our body’s melatonin levels will start to rise. Since we often use blue-light-emitting devices like screens — and just regular lamps! — at night, that natural process of melatonin production can be interrupted. That’s why blue-light-blocking glasses are a thing and where the idea for switching to red light comes in.

But when I asked Thomas if red light can actually help you sleep better, he suggested reframing the idea as red light is less likely to harm sleep via the circadian system. Using a red-light lamp at night before bed instead of a full-spectrum lamp may be less disruptive to your circadian rhythm, but it won’t do anything special beyond that, nor will it actively increase melatonin production. “You could also turn your lights down to a very dim lighting and do relaxation strategies for 30 minutes and achieve the exact same result,” Thomas explains. He advised thinking about red light for sleep as a way to minimize harm, rather than a strategy to improve sleep, “just like not drinking a pot of coffee before bed will help your sleep.”

It’s unlikely that using a red-light device for sleep would cause any ill effects. If you like having a red lamp on at night before bed and it makes you feel relaxed and sleepy, that’s a win in Thomas’s book. He does recommend keeping an eye on how bright your red lamp is, however, as brightness alone can be disruptive to your circadian rhythm, no matter what color the light is. And remember, nothing is better for your sleep than pure darkness — I’ve heard this over and over again from many sleep experts I’ve spoken to — so there is no benefit to leaving your red lamp on after you’ve fallen asleep.

Thomas also emphasized that if you’re having genuine difficulty with sleep, a visit to your doctor is always a good idea. No amount of futzing with your bedroom lighting can resolve serious sleep conditions like sleep apnea or insomnia.

According to Thomas, if you’re normally exposed to a lot of bright light in your living room or bedroom after sunset, and you find that is negatively impacting your sleep, using a red-light device would be reasonable. But it’s also not the first thing he’d recommend people spend their money on. Simply dimming the lights or reducing the overall brightness in your space is just as effective, he says. And making sure that you get enough exposure to bright blue light during the daytime, ideally from going outside, can help preserve your circadian rhythm so that you get enough sleep at night.

From my own experience testing red-light devices, I’m also a bit wishy-washy on whether they’re worth purchasing. The ones marketed as beneficial for sleep are essentially bedside lamps, and I tried two of them: the Melalight and the Helight. The Melalight is more of a straightforward lamp, while the Helight is smaller and designed to slowly fade out to mimic a sunset (the Melalight does have a timer feature but no option to fade gradually). The Melalight emits 660-nanometer wavelengths, and the Helight emits 630-nanometer wavelengths — both of which are in the red spectrum — and the two companies make similar claims about red-light’s connection to the circadian rhythm and how red light “supports” melatonin production.

Both the Melalight and Helight were significantly less bright than my regular bedside lamp and did create a vibe-y ambience in my bedroom. But their lack of brightness also made them not very functional as lamps. They weren’t bright enough to serve as a reading light or to light my bedroom while getting ready for bed, so I still had to use other lighting, which defeated the purpose of having red light. There simply isn’t a time before bed when I need an extremely dim light — I either want enough light to read or none at all. But between the two brands, I’d give a slight edge to the Melalight, as its larger size allows it to work better as a lamp that actually illuminates the room (especially if you have one on each side of the bed).

That’s not to say these lamps have no use. I occasionally find them useful on dark mornings when getting ready for the gym before work, as I can have a bit of light without waking up my husband. And if you like to meditate, stretch, or do another calming activity before bed that doesn’t require much light, they could be a nice way to help you get into a sleepy headspace. They could also be a nice accent light, like a Himalayan salt lamp. But given their price tags — the Melalight costs $169 and the Helight costs $139 — they likely aren’t worthwhile for most people who are looking to seriously improve their sleep.

entry.title: Mustard Made’s Very Last Sale of the Year Is Here
entry.summary: Everything is 25 percent off through November 11, including several of my personal favorites.
entry.content:
I’ve been a big fan of Mustard Made ever since it launched in the U.S. The brightly colored lockers and shelving units add some whimsy to my otherwise wood- and neutral-filled interiors. They’re also actually useful for storage — a must-have in my city apartment — thanks to the deep, adjustable shelves and a lock for valuables.

The lockers and accessories can be expensive, which is why I recommend waiting to shop during the company’s rare biannual sales. Through November 11, absolutely everything is 25 percent off. It’s the brand’s second and final sale of the year, so don’t delay — there probably won’t be another until Memorial Day 2027.

At just under 40 inches wide and 30 inches tall, this double locker would make a great small-space TV stand or home for a record player. Each side has one removable/adjustable shelf, and there’s also an opening for cables in the back. The matching baskets nestle inside smoothly, too.

I knew I needed this style as soon as it launched — I love how the translucent fluted glass offers a peek at what’s inside while still semi-obscuring some items. I think it would make a gorgeous bar cabinet, but the olive colorway is currently in my entryway and holds hats, scarves, sunglasses, and purses while still looking beautiful. At just over three feet tall, it’s also the perfect height for dropping off keys, shopping bags, and anything else I collect during errands.

The Midi was runner-up in my search for an entryway cabinet. It has the same details as the Lowdown — cable opening in the back, magnetic finish, and two keys for locking both sides — but is roughly twice the height and has two shelves per side. It’s an ideal unit for all-around storage, whether that’s toys in a kid’s room, office supplies, or pantry goods.

One of the brand’s original designs, the Skinny is useful for hanging clothes (there’s a hanging bar at the top, and the matching clothes hangers are designed to fit inside perfectly). It comes with four removable shelves. And the Skinny really is super-skinny, so one recommendation for more storage is buying a few different colors and lining them up.

On the other hand, you could just buy the Twinny, which is like two Skinnys pushed together.

The other original design is the Shorty, which would make a great low-profile nightstand, side table, or plant stand with storage, as pictured. It comes with two adjustable shelves and an interior hook, and there’s also a version that opens to the right, in case you want to line two up together.

The taller version of the Mixer lives in my dream kitchen or dining room — it’s the perfect alternative to a sideboard or credenza because the fluted-glass-covered shelves can store my collection of beautiful vases and serving platters without hiding them away from sight.

Another great all-around storage unit, the Standard is the lowest, widest option. But it still has plenty of room, as well as four included shelves and a cable hole.

This wall-mounted storage piece is useful for a bit of extra space in a kitchen or bathroom. I think it would be a great way to display a collection of novelty mugs — or just to hold extra toilet paper.

This grown-up version of a bulletin board (which can be hung vertically, too) would look beautiful in an office or kitchen, and you can also buy circle magnets in all of the colors to go with it.

Both this shelf and the larger version (33.5 inches long) are magnetic and can be configured the shelf on the bottom or top. Both hold around 30 pounds, so you can display books, candles, pottery, and more.

Growing up, our fridge was covered in letter magnets — these are just the grown-up version (which come in numbers, too).

entry.title: Everything I’d Buy From Nordstrom’s Extra Early Black Friday Sale
entry.summary: Including UGG slippers, candles, and a puffer for kids.
entry.content:
Holiday sales get earlier and earlier every year, and Nordstrom is following suit with a quick, very early Black Friday sale. Running now through November 11, a smallish selection of its clothing, beauty, and home sections are discounted. I pulled a number of recommendations, whether they’re Strategist-favorite brands, particularly good deals, or luxury items that rarely go on sale. Some of these products might get an extra markdown come November 27 — no promises, but you can always click the heart icon next to a listing to save it to your New York Magazine account for later.

For more Black Friday information, read senior deals editor Sam Daly’s guide to shopping all the sales and take a look at all the products we think will go on sale this year so you can be notified when prices drop.

As usual, the women’s clothing section is stuffed full of decent discounts. I like the selection of sweaters, from the kitschy dog print to the argyle cardigan. But the Marcella going-out top is also divine. Plus there are Birkenstock Bostons, UGG slippers, Adidas Sambas, and more.

There isn’t much on sale in the men’s department (sorry, guys). But I pulled a few nice items — a lovely coat for fall, pajamas that would make a decent gift, and a couple nice pairs of loafers for office-bound men.

The kids’ section has a ton of on-sale Nike, as well as one of our favorite puffer coats. I added a couple nice winterish shoes (plus one offseason Birkenstock). And for the babies, a highly recommended high chair and linen carrier.

Some of our favorite people’s favorite fragrances (and one of my own) are 15 percent off — not the lowest discount, but meaningful for higher-priced items. There are also a few nice Tom Ford lipsticks on sale, plus some of Kiehl’s thick, winter-friendly skin care.

The home and kitchen sale is surprisingly well stocked, with some Strategist-favorite brands like Our Place and Caraway. I’d also recommend taking a look at some of the home scents; I love my Kai diffuser!

entry.title: Iced Coffee and Skin-Care Hauls: The Best Advent Calendars for Gen Z (So Far)
entry.summary: Including one with enough Red Bull to get through finals season.
entry.content:
Gen Z might have it best when it comes to Advent calendars. They’re not quite kids and not quite adults, so there’s nothing stopping them from opening 24 days’ worth of coloring books or 12 days’ worth of “cheeky” Pink panties other than their wallet. (But, really, who’s to stop Gen-Xers from doing the same?) We’re still a ways away from actual Advent, but it feels like all the Advent calendars a Gen-Zer could want — from those filled with TikTok-famous beauty products to another with enough Red Bull to get through finals season — have already been available for weeks. I’ve been keeping track of each and every Advent calendar teens and young adults might want, and I’d recommend acting fast before they sell out. If you’re looking to peruse even more Advent calendar content, we have a big guide to all of this year’s best Advent calendars, along with dedicated guides to the best early beauty Advent calendars, food Advent calendars, fashion and jewelry Advent calendars, and Advent calendars for kids.

Update on November 5, 2026
﻿I added several Advent calendars, including new ones from Victoria’s Secret and Nespresso, and checked the price and availability of the others here.

Most of the beauty Advent calendars I’ve seen have at least a couple Gen-Z-loved beauty products, but Urban Outfitters’ calendar may as well have been designed by a high-schooler. There are Starface pimple patches (yes, the ones Gen Z wears out and about) and a travel-size bodywash from Sol de Janeiro. I also spotted a mini-version of the Billie Eilish perfume that topped wish lists last year.

The Sephora Advent calendar has been sold out for a couple weeks, but Ulta’s is still going strong. Inside, there are mini-versions of lots of viral products, including Sacheu’s lip-liner stain, some Benetint, and a pack of those buzzy Kardashian gummies (these ones are geared toward better digestion).

Revolve’s 25-day Advent calendar has fallen, but the 12-day version is still available. I’d say this one’s for the TikTok girlies — and, rest assured, there are full-size products inside. Ilia mascara or Sacheu eye shadow, anyone?

It’s the first year that Ipsy’s 25-day Advent calendar is available to everyone (rather than just those who have a subscription), and it’s full of mini and full-size products. The company has only revealed six items so far, but I spotted several full-size Gen-Z favorites: Gisou lip oil, Glow Recipe drops, and a tube of Too Faced Better Than Sex mascara.

When I interviewed shoppers at American Dream earlier this year, many teens told me they now preferred Alo over Lululemon. There’s a seven-day Advent calendar for those who agree that includes several of the brand’s wellness products and the claw clip on every girl’s wish list.

I’ve long said Dedcool’s nice-smelling detergent would make a nice gift for a college student, and the brand’s Advent calendar includes a travel-size version of the detergent that would be perfect for spring break. There are also some other purse-friendly staples — notably, a coconut lip balm and solid fragrance in one of the brand’s signature gourmand scents, Mochi Milk.

Laneige’s Advent calendar is a lip lover’s dream. There are no fewer than six lip products inside — that would be two lip serums, two lip glowy balms, and one lip sleeping mask.

Speaking of lip lovers — this one is dedicated to all things lips, and the Advent calendar itself is in the shape of a tube of lipstick. I think the Benetint, Make Up For Ever liner, and Kylie Cosmetics gloss would make for a nice lip combo.

It’s somewhat of a Gen-Z ritual to use a face mask at least once a week. Here’s an Advent calendar with ten masks and a couple of eye patches. Some are meant for soothing, while others target pore control or moisture, so you can bank them for 2027 or use them throughout the holiday season.

It’s been a few years since teens raided Sephora displays in search of Glow Recipe Dew Drops (and Drunk Elephant, too), but Gen Z still loves the brand. The 12-day calendar includes those famous drops in their original form and a tinted version.

E.l.f. regularly comes up during my conversations with teens, and its 24-day Advent calendar would make a nice gift for a teen who’s loyal to the brand. It includes some tried-and-true favorites, such as the daily cleanser and lip oil, along with two Advent calendar exclusives.

We’ve been experiencing a Victoria’s Secret renaissance as of late. The silk pajamas were a holiday hit with teens last year, and when I interviewed teens about their fragrance wish lists last month, they all wanted Victoria’s Secret fragrance mists and perfumes. This Advent calendar has a mix of both. Expect appearances from several Bombshell perfumes and mists along with some fun exclusives (a key chain and ornament, included).

We’re living amid the super dupes, and Dossier is a Gen-Z favorite for fragrance. The brand’s 12-day Advent calendar includes scents “inspired by” Le Labo’s Santal 33 and Tom Ford’s Vanilla Sex. There are some Dossier originals too.

Believe it or not Target, of all places, is where many teens go to discover new fragrances these days. The newly released scent-filled Advent calendar has several favorites, including the Athena Club body mist in Golden Vanilla and Eos’ body lotion in Fresh and Cozy.

ICYMI: Gen Z is still obsessed with all things Snoopy. With milk-chocolate toffee crunch and dark-chocolate mint squares, this chocolate Advent calendar is a step up from the no-frills ones from the grocery store.

There’s another Snoopy-forward one from Sugarfina. My boyfriend and I got the non-Snoopy version last year and loved trying all the different gummies. (My favorites, the passion fruit gummies and sweet-and-sour hearts, are in this one too.)

For those who have waited on line at BonBon, may I suggest an Advent calendar dedicated to Swedish candy from Sockerbit. It includes extra surprises on Saturdays (meaning bigger baggies stuffed with gummies). That should be the new standard.

I’ve made it somewhat of a tradition to watch as many dorm-tour videos as I can every August, and each year it feels like college students stuff their mini-fridges with more energy drinks than the last. I’ve only spotted this one from Red Bull so far, but I’d suggest Celsius and Alani Nu get on it, too.

Though if you’d prefer your caffeine in coffee form, there’s this one from Cometeer that’s filled with flash-frozen coffee. You can enjoy it hot or, well, iced for anyone who wants to bring iced coffee to their job interview …

For college kids who have a Nespresso machine in their dorm, there’s a Nespresso Advent calendar too (done in collaboration with none other than Swarovski). Each door has a new coffee pod, and there’s a branded tumbler at the end.

In New York pop-up history, Fishwife’s has felt as popular among my contemporaries as the ones by Parke and Pleasing. For those who couldn’t make it (and those who simply like tinned fish), the brand made an Advent calendar with its signature playful packaging. Inside, there are the usuals — smoked salmon, albacore tuna, and mussels — along with some fun mementos, like chocolate sardines and the company’s new collaboration with Bag Balm.

Fly by Jing makes some of my favorite fancy instant noodles (the other is from Momofuku), and its Advent calendar includes all the noodle flavors along with other spicy specialties.

For those who have made stationery the fixation of their 20s, Papier’s 12- and 24-day Advent calendars have all the fixings — roller-ball pens, highlighters, and thank-you cards included.

There’s also an embroidery Advent calendar for the 20-somethings who have picked up the hobby. Each day you embroider a new icon onto the calendar, which you can display at the end of the month.

I’ve been seeing Coco Wyo’s coloring books on lots of teen wish lists this year. Here’s an Advent calendar filled with 24 mini-versions of its coloring books.

If I were Snoopy, I’d be worried about Miffy stealing my fans. For those who have converted, there’s a 12-day Advent calendar filled with sticker sheets dedicated to the beloved bunny.

Pink is one of the latest additions to Tween Row, and I imagine the brand’s pantie Advent calendar will be a big hit with teens this year. It includes 12 limited-edition panties with festive bedazzled slogans like “Naughty” and “Nice.”

Victoria’s Secret made a slightly skimpier 12 Days of Thongs. Expect lots of bedazzled panties and lacy thongs.

Kendra Scott is still a top jewelry brand for teens and tweens (though Enewton is up there too). The brand’s 2026 Advent calendar has several viral products — including a couple of those pendant necklaces — available in either silver or gold, depending on your preference.

Between the brand’s pajamas and sweatshirts, teens can’t get enough of Skims. I’d expect the Advent calendar to go quickly; it has several fun accessories, like satin scrunchies, a faux-fur compact mirror, and a Skims squishy.

For our Swifties, I found an Advent calendar that comes with charms, beads, and chains to build their own bracelets.

Teen-loved mall brand Altar’d State has also made a charm bracelet Advent calendar. It has a gold-tone paper-clip chain and 12 mini-charms to put on it.

In case you were wondering: You’ll only find ankle socks in this Advent calendar.

Kitsch’s Advent calendar doesn’t include the viral zigzag headbands, but there are plenty of other festive hair accessories inside, like a cocoa-colored Cloud claw clip, pistachio-scented hair perfume, and white-as-snow satin pillowcase.

For about half the price of the Kitsch calendar, Conair’s has several clips and hair ties, too. The travel brush with a becharmed chain is also a fun touch.

entry.title: The Puffers, Parkas, and Rain Coats, and Vests We Buy for Our Kids
entry.summary: What Strategist editors’ children will be wearing this winter.
entry.content:
One of the most difficult parts of coat shopping for kids is finding the ones that will keep them warm and dry in all sorts of weather, while accounting for their often strong opinions about what looks nice and feels comfortable, while also not spending too much on something they could potentially lose and will eventually outgrow. It’s about that time of year again, so I talked to a bunch of Strategist parents, whose kids range in age from 13 weeks to 12 years old, about the coats they — and their children — like best.

“I like Patagonia kids’ clothing because it’s durable and holds its resale value well. I’ve been paying attention to the neighborhood parents’ group chats I’m in and almost everything ends up going for free or cheap except Patagonia outerwear. We bought this Reversible Down Sweater Hoody when our baby was about 10 weeks old and went with the 3–6 months size, knowing she’d grow into it by the time cold weather came around. She gets so cozy inside that she starts falling asleep. And I like that it’s reversible so we can change up her look for fun — or to hide stains. It’s definitely on the spendier side, but Patagonia even sells used versions on its site now, through its Worn Wear program. There’s currently one available for $83.”

“I got this parka from Reima for my 7-year-old last winter. I love the brand for its cold-weather clothing and already owned some of its snowsuits, rain jackets, fleeces, and boots, so I knew it would be well-made and warm. My son is on the smaller side for his age and I got him one size up — a size 7 when he was 6 — so he could wear it for at least two winters. It is down- filled and waterproof, covers his butt, has a bunch of pockets including warmers, and comes with a detachable and adjustable faux-fur-trimmed hood. He wears it all winter, including in snow storms and on the ski slopes. He and I both love this coat.”

“Both of my kids have worn a version of Zara’s down puffers, which are a fantastic value. They’re super-warm, cute, and durable. I have a couple hand-me-downs from his older brother in rotation for my 4-year-old.”

“I got this as a sample for my 4-year-old, and he wears this and the Zara coat throughout the winter. I love how warm and stylish it is. It’s a little bulky, but he has never complained about it.”

“Patagonia Hi-Loft is my favorite because it tends to come in great colors and stays lofted and puffy through a lot of wear. We generally wash these maybe once in the middle of winter and then again at the end of winter before putting them in storage. We have gotten one or two pieces secondhand and they, like the others, also wash and dry easily. The kids are happy to wear them and they stay very warm even in the coldest temperatures. We’ve had them in pretty much every size, including the baby bunting version.”

“This is our go-to transitional jacket. Apollo, who is 3.5 years old, has been wearing it every day this fall, as his older sister did with the same coat seven years ago. It’s ideal for 45-to-65 degree temperatures, especially if you layer at the lower end over a sweater or sweatshirt. It also washes really easily and dries well in the dryer. Apollo can unzip it and get it off himself. Best of all, these coats are extremely durable. We got ours secondhand from kids who are now 13 and 16 years old, so the coats are at least ten years old and have gone through multiple kids.”

“Lastly, we had a Patagonia Tribbles coat in a size 2T that both of my sons wore for around six months of cold weather each. It was extra cozy from the fleece, which can be worn on the inside or the outside, and it has an optional hood. It can handle colder temperatures if you layer up, and it washes very easily.”

“The Patagonia kids’ Torrentshell rain jacket is a solid three-season jacket. Not too heavy for a summer rain, but not too flimsy for shielding wind later into the fall.”

“This is lightest rain coat we own. It layers nicely over a sweater without adding much bulk or heat, or just alone with a tee on hotter, humid rainy days.”

“The Nano Puff is my daughter’s most-worn jacket. It gets almost constant wear in the spring and fall. It has a super-slim profile that keeps her warm without adding a lot of bulk — like in the car seat, for example.”

“This is one of the warmest kid’s coats I’ve handled. I was drawn to the longer length — it hits around the thighs and covers their butt. I also appreciate how high up it zips. The neck area always feels a little exposed in kids’ coats, but this one has a puffy band that acts almost like a scarf. My favorite part, though, is the shape of the hood, which reminded me of snorkel hoods that encircle the face. There’s a little bit of elastic, which keeps the hood secure — great when you can’t get a beanie on under there. Nice chunky zippers.”

“Reima’s Paimio down jacket is a great, solid puffer that’s a little heavier and longer than Patagonia’s Hi-Loft Down Sweater. It’s not as warm as the Reima Osteri, which feels like the coat they’re wearing on the most bitter-cold, blizzard-y days. This Reima style is a daily driver winter coat that still allows a lot of movement for play.”

“My son started out this fall wearing a navy blue Primary lightweight puffer jacket I bought for him one size too big last year. Then, halfway through October, it got left at the playground and disappeared. Now it’s on sale and I am seriously considering buying it again. It’s warm enough for most days until after Thanksgiving on the East Coast and great for kids who can’t stop moving because it’s light and breathable. He had the same lightweight puffer (but in green) in a size 2T that he wore from when he was about a year old to around 2.5 years old, and it held up well enough to be used by our friends’ kid for another two years after that. I love that it comes in a bunch of bright colors and washes really well without much effort.”

“As a backup, he’s been wearing this Cat & Jack puffer jacket that we got in a clothing swap from a neighbor, and I like it enough to keep sending him to school in it for the rest of the fall. It’s a tiny bit heavier than his Primary puffer because of the fleece lining, which also makes it extra cozy. But the fleece also sticks to other clothing a bit, where the Primary puffer is unlined and more slippery. So if I want to layer anything more than a long-sleeve tee underneath, I will have to size up.”

“We also have this packable lightweight puffer from 7am Enfant that is a touch lighter than the Primary lightweight puffer and about as warm with the added benefit of a pouch to pack it into that I lost at some point last winter. It’s very sleek looking and has nice details like front patch pockets that snap closed. Plus it’s thin enough to layer under a denim jacket. But it does run small compared to all of our other jackets, and the fit is boxy rather than long. My son is almost 4 years old now and wearing the size 3-4T, but he’ll soon grow out of it even though he is on the small side for his age.”

“I love this Reima rain coat because it’s totally waterproof with welded seams and because it’s flexible and breathable enough to be worn all day long, even while playing and climbing nonstop. It’s also durable, has reflective strips at the wrists and on the hood, and is extremely cute. My son had one in yellow that he wore from around 18 months to 3 years old. Now he has an orange one in a size 3T that is printed with Moomin characters and still fits him well.”

“I bought this faux-shearling vest on sale last winter in a size 4T and it is just now starting to fit my son without looking way too big. The fleece is thick and marshmallow-y and looks expensive. It’s been our go-to back-up that I pack on long days out when I’m not sure how cold it’ll get later in the day. And because it’s roomy, I can layer it over a lightweight puffer or a hooded sweatshirt and it keeps him super-warm. There’s a long-sleeved fleece-jacket version too that looks just as nice.”

“My 9-year-old son loves this coat, which used to be carried at Bloomingdales but is now only at a handful of online retailers. I’m going to buy it in a bigger size because he’s already told me he’s sad, anticipating that it’s now too small. It is a bright shiny red and incredibly warm (down with fleece lining), and it always looks clean and bright.”

“I refer to this as my son’s soccer jacket because it’s warm but highly flexible, so you can play sports outdoors in the winter comfortably while wearing it.”

“Both of my daughters have an extremely strong aversion to neutrals — these kids want their favorite colors over all else. Sometimes that can be hard to find! So we buy a lot of Boden coats, which always come in great colors and patterns. My 8-year-old will get at least another year out of a (no longer available) pink leopard-print Boden coat I bought last year that is kind of a mix between these two — padded and warm with a fleece lining, but also reversible if you want to wear the fleece on the outside. “

“Again with the favorite colors — Primary is another brand that reliably delivers on this front. My 8-year-old is on her second round of the Primary striped puffer jacket in pink and her third Primary puffer overall (I bought her first one, in solid pink, when she was around age 4). It’s her first-choice coat for most days because it’s not too bulky; she saves her Boden coat for colder weather or days when she’s not riding her bike to school. My 11-year-old previously wore one that was printed with rainbow stars, and she has a lavender-striped one on deck that I bought last year around this same time; November is definitely the best time to buy because Primary always starts its Black Friday sale early. So I’m not telling her they came out with a teal version this year — her favorite color — so she’ll actually wear it without asking for a new one.”

“Both of my kids wear have worn this Reima Sulkava rain jacket, albeit in a different color that’s no longer available. It’s especially nice when they are biking to school on wet days because it’s flexible and breathable, so they stay comfortable and don’t get too hot, but it’s still waterproof. It also layers well over the hoodies that my elder daughter vastly prefers to actual coats. After my sister saw one of my kids wearing it, she bought the same coat for my nieces, too.”

“Regarding the hoodies, the older kid wears one every day and always avoids adding a coat if possible, because in her mind, coats are only for the absolute coldest — or wettest — weather. Must of her hoodie wardrobe consists of overpriced and fairly lightweight tie-dye numbers we’ve bought at soccer tournaments. But she does have one Pink Palm Puff hoodie (Everything Comes in Waves in blue) that she absolutely adores. It may no longer be the bastion of coolness with older girls, but I have to admit, it is really nicely made and didn’t cost much more than the soccer-tournament merch. It’s weighty and warm and, for her, it’s a perfectly acceptable ‘coat’ in cooler fall weather.”

“Nonetheless, said older kid does still need a new warmer coat, and I’m waffling between the Reima Paimio that Simone has and this one that’s very spiritually similar to the lighter Sulkava above — the waterproof ReimaTec fabric is just so nice and flexible, and this coat has insulation for colder temperatures. Since it’s technically a ski jacket, the ‘helmet-compatible hood’ should also work for biking to school.”

entry.title: What Commuter-Friendly Shoes Are All the Cool People Wearing?
entry.summary: “Now when I put them on, I feel like my feet say a little thank-you.”
entry.content:
My commute to the New York office includes a car trip, a ride on NJ Transit, and five stops on the subway. I’ve learned the hard way that you can’t brave a gravelly Central Jersey parking lot, angry crowds at Penn Station, and juicy curb puddles of Fidi in just any pair of shoes. But even as office dress codes have loosened, few want to sit at a desk in practical thick-soled sneaker sneakers. So in search of actually attractive footwear that can withstand shoulder-to-shoulder schleps through bustling transit hubs, I asked stylish commuters about the professional-looking shoes they wear to work. Their answers run the spectrum of office dress codes, and most will take you from day to night (fulfilling the dream outlined on every other page of an early-aughts Marie Claire). Here, you’ll find everything from walkable Weejuns to Repettos for Citi Bike–ing. And if you’re looking for more work-appropriate shoes, we have guides to the best flats and mary janes.

Sandy Sanchez, a copywriter and writer of the Small Pleasures newsletter, prefers to avoid transferring train lines in favor of a slightly longer walk from the station. That preference is made possible by the (aptly named) Jeffrey Campbell Trustees. “It’s nice knowing I don’t have to worry about my feet hurting when I wear them,” says Sanchez. (They get a break at work: “I’m at my desk most of the day, so I’m really just wearing these shoes to and from the fridge to restock on sparkling water and from meetings to meetings.”) There are approximately 54 minutes of walking total on her commute, and “that’s on days I don’t have anything before or after work.”

While recovering from a major ankle surgery that required “responsible arch-support shoes that weren’t Hokas,” Anne Whiting, a writer and communications strategist, discovered the Dansko Linden. Just in time for working in a very conservative (“like, navy-blue tailored suits everywhere”) office environment. As a freelancer, she may be “all over the city” at any given time: “A work event at MoMA PS1, a meeting in Soho, a walk to a coffee shop near home, a schlep to dinner at Dumbo House.” At least two hours of her day are spent in trains and climbing up and down stairs. But she can wear the Lindens with a suit for a “more buttoned-up client in midtown” or just to film a social-media video elsewhere. No matter what she’s carrying (a laptop, lunch, a camera, gym clothes, groceries), her Lindens “withstand the volume and the miles and take the fear away that I’m hurting my bunions or arches or something. You just feel … supported.” Plus your toes aren’t forced into “some pointed submission.” She adds, “When I put them on, I feel like my feet say a little thank-you.”

Alisha Bansal, who works at Christie’s and runs the Weird Real, heard about Franco Sarto’s Bocca on the Strategist; a recommendation from Wall Street Journal art editor Alexandra Citrin-Safadi in our loafers guide. “They are essentially orthopedic The Row,” says Bansal. “My feet aren’t killing me by the end of the day.” She takes the subway for about 45 minutes to midtown every day for work, and with these shoes, she doesn’t “need to feel too precious about them or feel bad if they get beat up or rained on, etc.” Especially as they’re relatively cheap and “more substantial than flats.”

Marketing consultant Lizzie Noonan couldn’t believe she found new, in-box Pêche Hughs at a closet sale and “timidly asked what was wrong with them, convinced they must be uncomfortable or that I was missing something” — only to be assured they were just the wrong size for the previous owner. “They’ve been as comfortable as sneakers from the get-go, no painful break-in period or emergency flat swap at the office,” Noonan says. Going between Fort Greene to Fidi regularly, “which on any given day involves a mad dash for the elusive G train,” they’ve also survived a flash flood — “the kind that turns NYC streets into one big lazy river” and even gone on vacation to the British countryside. “Once someone asked if they were The Row, arguably the highest compliment there is,” she adds.

Nearly every day, Aisha Joshi, writer of the newsletter Babyteeth, has to do a ten-minute walk and transfer between the L and the 1 at Sixth Avenue that “always feels like the longest walk of my life.” Twice a week, she commutes in the Sammies. Working at a beauty start-up, she finds herself “on random missions to the Garment District for ribbon or BeadKraft” or just running to a photo shoot in them. “Sometimes my feet hurt after even ballet flats, and these are gentler on my feet — plus there’s more toe space,” Joshi says. If needed, they can also easily fit inside a tote.

Sometimes Produce Parties founder Sarah Teich’s commute doesn’t go as planned — including recently when “the L was down, the G was running slow, the F was delayed, and everyone was pushing and shoving.” At least her feet don’t hurt when she’s in the Hollies. They remind her of a sneaker: “comfy all day while I rush from meeting to meeting to meeting.”

Catbird chief creative officer Leigh Plessner’s morning routine goes something like this: “I take the L train two stops to drop my daughter at school, stop for a macchiato, and then walk two miles from Williamsburg into the back gate of the Brooklyn Navy Yard to our studio.” And “when I need to dart around quickly,” she brings Air Rifts. They make her “feel elegant and unexpected and in control” — like even when she needs to speed-walk, “the world is my oyster.” Better yet, “I love when I surprise a colleague with them who doesn’t expect me to be secretly sporty/sci-fi (I’m not; they are right),” she says.

Bria Schirripa, the chief of staff at a financial institution and writer of the newsletter Friend Of, has been commuting in the same checkered Vans longer than she’s been with her husband — over 11 years. “The bottoms are completely worn down, but if I know it’s going to be a bad commute or the weather is terrible, I throw them on.” Then she changes into another pair of Vans she keeps at her desk. “It’s kind of crazy, but I don’t want to dirty them,” she says of this “nicer pair.”

Gabriela Peralta, the social-media manager at the Guggenheim, commutes via the LIRR and transfers on the MTA. Her New Balance 1906Ls keep up with “a lot of walking, stairs, and running between trains.” Once, when all the stairways to get a downtown 4 train were blocked, she had to find her way to the other side of the 86th Street station: “When you’re already an hour into your commute, having to navigate around a hot station like that is not ideal,” says Peralta. “I was especially grateful to be wearing comfortable shoes.” Her average day may include anything from a social shoot at the Guggenheim (or just going up and down the quarter-mile-long spiral) or an early-morning preview at the Met. “I can wear them through a busy day without my feet feeling worn out,” she says.

“I’m one of few privileged New Yorkers who commute to work on foot (door-to-door about 25 minutes; under 20 if I’m booking it),” says Audrey Lee, a shopping editor at Architectural Digest. Her shoes have to be “utilitarian enough to keep me agile” and stylish so she can avoid having to “pack a spare pair in my already overstuffed work bag.” G.H.Bass’s Whitney Weejuns fit the bill nicely. “In my line of work, lots of events tend to be standing only, which means I’m previewing the newest Danish chairs or Scandi sofas with nary a viable seat in sight — ironic, I know,” says Lee. “These make it easy to listen to designers monologue about the trip to Prague that influenced their latest ceramics without my feet feeling like they’re about to fall off.” Fair warning: Because of the “delicate pony hair, a rainy-day shoe these are not.”

Schirippa’s Prince Street ballet flats have “literally made it through a million subway delays and reroutes that have forced me to walk home farther than I ever intended.” But the most “traumatic incident for the flats” happened when the F train stopped because “someone in a car in front of us had pulled the emergency brake,” forcing passengers to walk through subway cars back to the previous station. “Bergen Street to Carroll Street is a 12-minute walk above ground, but walking through the subway cars felt like it took hours,” she says. “Everyone was completely silent because we were all so annoyed.” She credits the Prince Street flats for getting her through the experience — and posted about the saga on Instagram, tagging Alex Mill and asking, “When you made these flats, did you intend for them to be used to walk underground through the subway?” (Alex Mill replied to her story with “U are the vision.”) No wonder why she has them in blue and purple now, in addition to red. “Some people throw on sneakers to run out and run errands. I throw on these flats,” she tells me.

Brand manager Sarah Veurink switches between commutes depending on her mood: “I live by Barclays Center, so the options are really endless — some days it’s the B to C, others it’s the 2 to 1, and when I feel like walking it’s the Q all the way.” Luckily, her Loeffler Randall Coopers have been up for anything, including a time when she zoned out, took the N to Queens, and had to run around Queensboro Plaza to get back to Manhattan for a 9:30 a.m. meeting. “I was totally expecting horrible blisters, but it’s been the opposite,” says Veurink. “The thick sole provides so much more protection from the ground than a normal ballet flat or mary jane.”

Tangerine and Nu Swim’s Gina Esposito bikes from Bed-Stuy to the East Williamsburg store in these Ballerette ballerinas frequently. “I’ve never had any knee or hip issues, which I usually have with other shoes that aren’t sneakers or flip-flops,” she says.

“My commute is always from Red Hook, so nothing is close or easy, often with a stop in Boerum Hill or Park Slope for Pilates or Noho for yoga before landing in LES,” says Jess Hella, owner of Yesterday Tomorrow. Her Repetto Cendrillon can handle the “mix of Citi Bike–ing, walking, and the subway.” She adds, “My worst commute in recent history involved a popped tire when biking to yoga when coming off the Brooklyn Bridge. It required me to walk the heavy Citi Bike with all of my bags to the nearest station, which was not so near.” It was a “truly humbling experience for 8 a.m,” but she “didn’t question” having on her Cendrillons. Plessner also describes them as “just a very, very flat shoe to slip my foot in and go go go.”

Saloon’s Julia Harrison’s office commute includes a two-block walk to the Bergen F and a transfer at Jay Street to the A. “All things considered,” it’s not bad — and she reaches for her Aldous loafers biweekly for the trip. “Unfortunately — but maybe fortunately for me — I can’t remember any particularly horrifying commute story I experienced in these loafers,” Harrison adds. “What I do know is that on certain floors (like the marble ones into the Oculus), they have little friction, so especially when they’re newer and not so worn in by the gritty New York pavement, they can slide a bit.” It’s a small price, as “they’re one of the few shoes I have that don’t make ghastly noise walking,” she says.

“To me, a good commuter shoe is comfortable to walk in, covers my heels and toes, and doesn’t slip off easily,” says artist Melly Wirtes. Her commute is “normally pretty tame:” a 6 train straight down the Upper East Side to Grand Central with a few blocks of walking (including “pretty hilly” Carnegie Hill). And the Uma Mary-Jane strap keeps her feeling secure throughout — even when she was caught in one of August’s torrential downpours: “I left work early and rushed to doggy day care. Alas, I did not beat the rain and my dog — a dachshund — demanded to be carried.” Yet, “feet fully wet, puddles to my ankles,” the Umas survived. “I propped them upside down to dry, and there isn’t any noticeable difference from before at all,” she says.

“At the office, I glide around in them like I’m still working from home,” says Noonan of Emme Parsons’ Parker. “I try to keep them pristine, though I know the day will come when they meet some type of only-in-NYC calamity.” Aside from “a few strangers stepping on my toes on a crowded subway,” they remain in good shape, she says.

Vanessa Krooss, head of brand at Merit, thinks she’s “legally obliged to own a pair” of Tabis as a Brooklynite. Every time she wears them, she gets asked something to the effect of “Ugh, should I buy a pair?” by a co-worker. But there’s a reason why they’re a staple. “I live in Park Slope and commute up to Nomad, so it’s usually around two trains (either the B, Q, or F to the 6) and 45-ish minutes if all goes well. Unfortunately, sometimes things do not go well,” she says. Like the time she had to walk ten blocks to Atlantic-Pacific in the rain and hop on three different lines to the office — only to realize she left her laptop at home. “Thankfully, I was wearing my trusty Tabis, which have been completely molded to my foot and recently resoled, so the standing-room-only trains and inclement weather weren’t an issue,” she says.
